sourceClaimMap.claim: The security property alone does not establish whether a loan is for personal, household, residential-investment or business purposes.
ASIC explains that the laws and borrower protections differ depending on the purpose of the loan.
The Australian Government's business-loan guide recommends comparing the loan term, interest rate, setup costs, ongoing fees and security, and preparing financial records and forecasts.
Business cash flow, lease income, financial statements, forecasts and the transaction plan may all need to be documented
A Key Facts Sheet sets out standard cost and feature information for comparison
Interest rate, comparison rate, fees, repayment type, features and loan term can be compared in a standard format
Consumer-credit protections may apply to regulated residential lending
Property can be at risk if the agreed repayments are not made.
Commercial property finance often requires the lender to understand both the borrower and the asset.

For residential home-loan comparison, Moneysmart points readers to the repayment method and frequency, interest-rate type, rate, fees, features, total amount to be repaid and monthly repayment shown in a Key Facts Sheet.
Business.gov.au lists financial reports, cash-flow statements, forecasts, identification, business plans and relevant agreements among the documents a lender may request.
A lower headline rate does not necessarily mean a lower total cost.
ASIC's current credit advertising guidance calls for a balanced account of benefits, risks and limitations.
